results.message: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
He was a real man, not an idea. One of us, Ignatius, wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and put it as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way those Ignatius wrote against claimed. And Ignatius said he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup, we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. More than one of our own households uses those words, not only Ignatius's own. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. We should say plainly, though: even in our own time, that chain was already felt as something thinning, not something we could simply rely on. The emperor once sent for some of Jesus' own family - grandsons of Judas, who was called his brother. What he found were two farmers with calloused hands. They told him about a kingdom not of this world, and he let them go. That is how close we still were, and how far.

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
One of us, Ignatius, calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

sources.work: The First Apology; c. 153-157 CE per Minns and Parvis (Oxford, 2009) - the best-anchored dating in this world's entire source set

sources.author: The 'Anonymous' anti-Montanist (writing c. 192-193 CE to Avircius Marcellus), preserved only in Eusebius's quotations; ANF prints the fragments under the conjectural name 'Asterius Urbanus'
sources.work: Fragments against the Montanists (the New Prophecy) - the earliest sustained inside-the-window testimony to Montanism's Phrygian origin, its spread, and the synodical opposition of Asia Minor's churches; the movement's start date is disputed between c. 157 (Epiphanius) and c. 172 (Eusebius's implied chronology), with current scholarship favoring the later end

sentences.sentence: One of us, Ignatius, calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them.
It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: But it is worship, not an argument worked out.
sentences.why: tagged claim, shares ground with its own records

sentences.sentence: How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out.
We can tell you plainly that we called him God.
We cannot tell you we had settled how.
We believed in one God, maker of everything.
But if you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature.
